title: A year on the porch
hook: a year with Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus

segments.voice: Yesterday: what you leave, with Epicurus as a guide, one idea set down fairly. Your line was not for me. Did you write it beside your three, with one kind sentence? Day six hundred eighty-nine.

A merchant from Cyprus named Zeno has been shipwrecked and lost his cargo. Stranded in Athens, he wanders into a bookshop and hears someone reading about Socrates. He asks the bookseller: where can I find men like that? The story goes that a philosopher happened to walk past right then, and the bookseller pointed. Years later, Zeno began teaching in a public colonnade on the edge of the marketplace. That covered walkway gave the school its name, and gave this whole year its name too. Today: a year on the porch.
screen: `A SHIPWRECKED MERCHANT.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THAT?` → `A COLONNADE IN ATHENS.`

segments.voice: First, the porch itself. In Greek, stoa poikilē: the painted porch, a long roofed walkway whose walls carried famous paintings, including the battle of Marathon. Anyone could walk in. Zeno taught there, in public, and his followers were called the people of the stoa: Stoics. A philosophy named not after a founder but after a public place where anyone could stand and listen. Second, the road we walked. We started on day three hundred thirty-two with a little handbook, Epictetus's teaching boiled down by his student Arrian, meant to be kept at hand. Then the longer Discourses, Epictetus arguing and joking with his students. Then Seneca, letter by letter, essay by essay. Then all twelve books of Marcus, straight through. And lately, the wider porch: the founders before, the neighbors next door, the people who came after, the turning year, and the porch in ordinary life. Third, four very different voices. A merchant who lost everything at sea. A man once enslaved, who limped. A rich adviser at a dangerous court. An emperor writing to himself on campaign. They didn't agree on everything, and they weren't saints. But each of them kept asking the same plain questions: what is up to me? What is good? How should I live with other people? Fourth, what a year does. One lesson is a thought. A year of them is a road, with your own days woven through it. Before we thank each teacher by name, it's worth looking back at where you started, and seeing how far the porch has run.
screen: `STOA POIKILĒ: THE PAINTED PORCH.` · `HANDBOOK, DISCOURSES, LETTERS, NOTEBOOK.` · `FOUR VOICES, THE SAME PLAIN QUESTIONS.` · `A YEAR OF DAYS, WOVEN IN.` · then, large: `A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: Go back, in your mind or in your notes, to day three hundred thirty-two, the handbook for the road. Its line was keep it at hand. What were you carrying then? What was hard in your life? Now look at today. What's changed, even slightly? Maybe nothing obvious; that's honest too. Then let the year's voices pass by, Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus, and notice which one, if any, you'd most like to sit beside. The bell holds the time.
Stoa poikilē, the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught in public, open to anyone who walked in off the street. Today's word.
Your line: what is up to me. If you kept notes this year, reread the first page today. If not, write one sentence about what the year gave you. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some people finishing a year of Stoic reading reread their earliest notes and ask how the practice has changed them, if at all.

original.note: Greek: the painted porch in Athens, where Zeno taught.

trapdoor: what you thought: stoic just means calm and unemotional.
what it means: the name comes from a public porch in Athens, where a school of practical philosophy began.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 7.2–5 tells of Zeno's shipwreck, the bookshop, Crates, and teaching in the Stoa Poikilē; Pausanias describes its paintings of Marathon.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: Zeno's shipwreck (purple dye cargo), the bookshop reading of Xenophon's Memorabilia 2, and Crates passing by: Diogenes Laërtius 7.2–3. Told as 'the story goes'. Confirm.
Zeno began teaching in the Stoa Poikilē around 300 BC: confirm date framing.
Paintings in the Stoa Poikilē included the battle of Marathon (Pausanias 1.15). Confirm.
The year's structure (Handbook from day 332, Discourses, Seneca, Meditations, wider porch) follows the y2 outline.
